summary: This work demonstrates single-step generation of W states in superconducting qubit lattices by engineering time-independent Hamiltonians that coherently distribute a single excitation across arbitrary geometries. In 2D lattices, simultaneous propagation along multiple directions reduces entanglement time to scale with the largest dimension, enabling a six-qubit W state with 83.9±1.0% fidelity in 99 ns on a 3×2 array and a seven-qubit W state with 79.6±1.3% fidelity in 264 ns.
motivation: W states are resilient to local loss and measurement, making them valuable for quantum communication and sensing. Sequential two-qubit gate approaches suffer from large circuit depth in systems with limited connectivity, motivating development of parallel single-step protocols using engineered simultaneous interactions.
method: Parametric AC flux drives applied to tunable couplers induce effective $XY$-type interactions within the single-excitation manifold. The required Hamiltonian parameters are determined by solving the inverse eigenvalue problem $e^{-i\hat{H}\tau/\hbar}|q_{\mathrm{centre}}\rangle = |W_N\rangle$, with closed-loop optimization of drive frequencies and amplitudes. For 2D square lattices, independent 1D Hamiltonians along each direction are combined to exploit parallel excitation propagation.
result: Genuine multipartite entanglement confirmed via witness operators for all instances. Maximum achievable couplings ranged from 1.8 to 3.5 MHz (median 2.2 MHz). Dominant errors were dephasing (8.7% for 3×2 case) and unmitigated state preparation and measurement errors (~7.7% higher excitation population). The 3×2 implementation outperformed any feasible 1D six-qubit operation in the device, demonstrating the speedup from multidimensional parallelism.
